doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Playing with Bobby Hutcherson and other soloists
summary: He explains how accompanying vibes, piccolo bass, trombone or piano changes the color of his playing though not his time.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Tell me about working with Bobby Hutcherson.
What do you want to know?
Well is it different playing behind—

The texture. The texture is different. Saxophone player, that’s a reed. When you have a bar that’s vibrating that’s different. If the guy out in front is like Ron Carter playing his piccolo bass that’s a different timbre. I’ve done those. I’ve played with Ron as the bass player and it’s fun. I enjoyed it. But it’s different. Piano trio or piano-led band is different. Trombone-led, like if you work with Steve Turre for instance, the timbre is different. You do make an adjustment but I’m sure the adjustment is a very subtle one. In terms of where you place time or stuff like that, there’s no change from that. But there are color changes, yes. I would definitely say that there’s some kind of a difference. And even with individual instruments. If I were to take the gigs I play with Bobby Hutcherson, the gigs I played with Milt Jackson, the gigs I played with Steve Nelson, they all have such individual personalities, although they’re all in that, you know it’s like Bags evolved into Bobby Hutcherson evolved into Steve Nelson. So even though there’s that common thread they’re from the same trunk — from the same branch of the trunk. Their individual styles are so — the color of their music — I was going to say the color of their notes, but it’s really the color of their music is so different that you play — there are some very, very subtle changes that you make in your music. What they are I can’t tell you.

But I don’t have the same template with everybody that I play with. I don’t. I don’t use the same — I use the same approach in terms of I’m Ray Drummond who feels this way and who hears this way and I do that consistently. But the name of that game, I mean the range of that game is totally dependent on the music itself, the selections, the kind of music that we’re going to play. Because I love all kinds of music. And just to start with

jazz alone, I won’t even get into the things I like to listen to but I don’t want to play, but jazz — and I’ve got some funny stories with respect to how in one sense it’s been kind of a labor to expand my — not just understanding — but my appreciation of musics that — I’ll give you examples.
